goldens.comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

The nullable field creates an enabled-without-backup-codes state but the feature provides no transition from that state to enabled-with-codes: every account that already has twoFactorEnabled=true remains null, login returns MissingBackupCodes, and setup rejects that same user at apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts:42-44, so the recovery path and its instruction to generate codes in settings are impossible for the users who need it; trigger/consequence: an existing 2FA user loses the authenticator and selects Lost access, then cannot obtain a code or reach a legal regeneration transition; state-model simplification advisory: make backup-code issuance/regeneration an explicit transition available to enabled accounts rather than an incidental side effect of first-time TOTP setup; strongest counterargument: users can disable and re-enable 2FA, but disable itself requires the unavailable TOTP or backup code and therefore cannot repair this state; deletion test: delete setup-only ownership of generation at apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts:60-68 and the MissingBackupCodes dead end at packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts:137 once an enabled-account regeneration transition owns issuance.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real state-model issue: existing users with twoFactorEnabled=true will have backupCodes=null after migration. The diff shows: 1) Migration adds nullable backupCodes column (line 1-2 of migration.sql), 2) Backup codes are only generated during setup (setup.ts:60-68), 3) Login with backup code throws MissingBackupCodes if user.backupCodes is null (next-auth-options.ts:137), 4) Setup endpoint rejects users who already have 2FA enabled (setup.ts:42-44 checks twoFactorEnabled). This creates an unrecoverable state for existing 2FA users who lose their authenticator - they cannot use backup codes (none exist), cannot regenerate them (setup rejects enabled accounts), and cannot disable 2FA (requires TOTP or backup code). The 'disable and re-enable' workaround mentioned in the finding is correctly identified as impossible.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/components/settings/EnableTwoFactorModal.tsx:135 — [P2; confidence 75] "setStep(SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes);" Backup-code delivery is split across an early setup response, browser-only component state, and a later enable commit, so a reload, tab loss, or lost enable response after the server enables 2FA leaves active stored codes that were never displayed and cannot be retrieved or regenerated; trigger/consequence: enable succeeds at the server but this post-response state transition never runs, and the newly enabled user permanently loses the only copy exposed by the product; lifecycle simplification advisory: display and acknowledge the already-generated codes before the enable commit, eliminating the post-commit dependency on volatile React state; strongest counterargument: holding codes in state avoids a second server response, but that convenience is precisely what makes successful persistence and successful delivery diverge; deletion test: delete the handleEnable post-success display transition at lines 134-136 and make the DisplayBackupCodes step follow handleSetup before QR/TOTP confirmation, so no enabled state depends on a later in-memory reveal.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real race condition in the 2FA enable flow. Looking at the diff: 1) In setup.ts (lines 60-75), backup codes are generated and stored encrypted in the database during the setup phase, and returned to the client. 2) In EnableTwoFactorModal.tsx, these codes are stored in React state (setBackupCodes at line 92). 3) The enable endpoint (handleEnable) is called separately, and only after it succeeds (line 132-136) does setStep(SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes) get called to show the codes. The problem: if the enable API call succeeds but the browser crashes, tab closes, or network issues prevent the response from being processed, the user's 2FA is now enabled with backup codes stored in the database, but the user never saw those codes (they were only in volatile React state). The codes were generated at setup time but only displayed after enable succeeds - this is a genuine architectural flaw where server-side persistence and client-side display can diverge.

Looking at the code, when 2FA is enabled, backup codes are displayed in SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes with options to close, copy, or download. adjudication.rationale: The diff shows backup code verification in next-auth-options.ts at lines 128-157. The code reads backupCodes, decrypts them, checks if the supplied code exists with indexOf, then updates the database to mark it as used. This is indeed a non-atomic read-check-write pattern: two concurrent requests with the same backup code could both read the same list, both pass the indexOf check (finding the code valid), and both authenticate successfully before either write completes. This is a real race condition vulnerability that allows a one-time backup code to be used multiple times.

If clipboard access is denied (permissions, secure context issues, etc.), the writeText call will fail but the success toast will still display unconditionally. For backup codes that are single-use recovery material, this is a real bug - users could believe they copied the codes when they didn't, then close the dialog and lose access to their account.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts:149 — [P1; confidence 100] "await prisma.user.update({" the read-check-write consumption is not atomic, so one backup code is accepted more than once; two concurrent credential requests using the same unused code both validate the same stored array before either unconditional update and both receive authenticated sessions, breaking the promised exactly-once access control.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a race condition in the backup code validation logic. Looking at the diff in next-auth-options.ts lines 128-160, the code: 1) reads backupCodes from the database, 2) decrypts and parses them, 3) checks if the supplied code exists in the array, 4) sets the code to null, 5) updates the database. Between steps 1-3 (validation) and step 5 (update), there's no transaction or atomic operation. Two concurrent requests with the same backup code could both pass validation before either update completes, allowing the same backup code to be used twice. This violates the stated security property that 'Each backup code can be used exactly once'.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts:149 — [P1; confidence 100] "await prisma.user.update({" backup-code consumption is an unconditional read/modify/write, so two concurrent authorize calls can validate the same pre-update list and both succeed, while concurrent uses of different codes can last-write-wins resurrect one consumed code; simultaneous submissions against one account violate the advertised exactly-once behavior and leave persisted consumption state inconsistent.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a race condition in the backup code consumption logic at lines 128-152 of next-auth-options.ts. The code reads backupCodes, checks if the user-supplied code exists in the array (indexOf), then sets that index to null and writes back. Two concurrent requests could both read the same backupCodes array before either writes, both find the same valid code, and both succeed - violating the 'exactly once' guarantee stated in the UI text. This is a real concurrency bug in the authentication flow that could allow a backup code to be used multiple times.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that password verification is skipped when using backup codes, but examining the code flow in next-auth-options.ts shows that password verification happens at lines 117-125 BEFORE the two-factor check at line 128. The code structure is: 1) verify password (lines 117-125), 2) then check 2FA with backup code OR TOTP (lines 128+). The password check uses 'isCorrectPassword' and throws 'IncorrectPassword' error if it fails. The backup code branch at line 128 only executes AFTER password verification has already passed. The finding incorrectly claims line 121 'skips verifyPassword' but that's not how the code flow works - password verification is a prerequisite before any 2FA check.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the test at line 116 only verifies the filename of the downloaded backup codes file, not its contents. Looking at the diff, the test does `expect(download.suggestedFilename()).toBe('cal-backup-codes.txt')` but has a TODO comment 'check file content' indicating the content verification is incomplete. The backup codes are critical for account recovery, and the download path creates a separate Blob from the backupCodes array (lines 93-97 in EnableTwoFactorModal.tsx). While the UI renders the same codes, the download blob construction is a separate code path that could potentially fail without the test catching it. This is a legitimate test coverage gap for newly added functionality, not a bug but an important missing test case.
